summary: Provides test vectors for HMAC combined with the SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 hash functions, which implementers can use to check conformance. It also gives ASN.1 object identifiers and URIs so protocols can name these schemes. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: If you bake a cake from a recipe, you want to know what it should look like. This memo gives the right answers for some secret-code recipes so programmers can check theirs.

questions: what are the object identifiers for hmac-sha-2
what is the block size of sha-512
how do i test my hmac implementation
subtitle: Official names and known-answer test cases for HMAC with SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512.

tldr.problem: Protocols need unambiguous names for HMAC combined with the SHA-2 hash functions, and implementers need known-correct answers to check their code against.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC allocates ASN.1 object identifiers and algorithm URIs for the four schemes and lists seven test cases with keys, data and expected HMAC values.
tldr.outcome: An implementation that matches the published results should interoperate with other implementations. The RFC makes no claim about how secure the schemes are for any use.

today: RFC 4231 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2005. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What This Document Provides
sections.content:
RFC 4231 provides test vectors for four message authentication schemes: HMAC-SHA-224, HMAC-SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-384 and HMAC-SHA-512. It also provides ASN.1 object identifiers and Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) that identify use of these schemes in protocols.

The ASN.1 identifiers are meant for protocols such as those built on S/MIME, and the URIs for protocols based on XML, such as those using XML Digital Signatures. The test vectors may be used for conformance testing.
sections.eli5: This memo gives each secret-code recipe an official name tag and a set of answer-key examples to test against.

sections.title: The Four HMAC-SHA Schemes
sections.content:
Each scheme is the realization of the HMAC message authentication code from RFC 2104 using one of the SHA-2 hash functions. HMAC-SHA-224 uses SHA-224, HMAC-SHA-256 uses SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-384 uses SHA-384 and HMAC-SHA-512 uses SHA-512. The hash functions themselves are described in the NIST Secure Hash Standard, FIPS 180-2.

The block size matters for the test cases. The RFC states it as 64 bytes for SHA-224 and SHA-256, and 128 bytes for SHA-384 and SHA-512. Several test cases deliberately use keys or data larger than a block.
sections.eli5: It is the same secret-mixing trick every time. Only the scrambling machine inside changes, and each has its own size.

sections.title: Scheme Identifiers
sections.content:
The object identifiers are allocated under rsadsi, which is {iso(1) member-body(2) us(840) rsadsi(113549)}. The branch digestAlgorithm is {rsadsi 2}, and the four schemes sit beneath it: id-hmacWithSHA224 as 8, id-hmacWithSHA256 as 9, id-hmacWithSHA384 as 10 and id-hmacWithSHA512 as 11.

When the algorithm component of an ASN.1 AlgorithmIdentifier names one of these schemes, the parameter component SHOULD be present but have type NULL.

Four URIs are also allocated, one for each scheme, ending in #hmac-sha-224, #hmac-sha-256, #hmac-sha-384 and #hmac-sha-512. In the XML Signature context, the ds:HMACOutputLength element may specify a truncated output length.
sections.eli5: Computers need a precise name for each recipe. A numbered address like 8, 9, 10 and 11 in a big directory does that job.

sections.title: The Test Vectors
sections.content:
Seven test cases follow, with keys, data and digests given in hex. Each case lists the expected output for all four schemes. Cases 1 and 2 are basic: case 1 uses a 20-byte key and the data "Hi There", and case 2 uses the key "Jefe", shorter than the HMAC output.

Cases 3 and 4 use a combined key and data length larger than 64 bytes. Case 5 tests truncation of the output to 128 bits. Case 6 uses a 131-byte key, larger than the 128-byte block size of SHA-384 and SHA-512. Case 7 uses that same size of key plus data that is also larger than the block size, so the key must be hashed before use.
sections.eli5: The test cases are like practice questions with the answers in the back of the book. Some are easy and some are tricky, like very long keys.

sections.title: Using the Vectors for Conformance
sections.content:
The test vectors were cross-verified by three independent implementations. An implementation that agrees with the results in this document should be interoperable with other similar implementations.

The test cases are derived from those in RFC 2202, which covers HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA-1, although the keys and data are slightly different.
sections.eli5: If three different people solved the puzzle and got the same answer, you can trust the answer key. If yours matches, your code works with theirs.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document only supplies identifications and test vectors. It makes no assertion about the security of these message authentication code schemes for any particular use. For the general security of the HMAC construction, the reader is referred to RFC 2104.
sections.eli5: This memo gives you the answer key, not a promise that the recipes are safe for every job.
